Reproducing the CalMS21 dataset paper (Sun et al. 2021) from dandiset 001878¶

Paper. Sun JJ, Karigo T, Chakraborty D, Mohanty SP, Wild B, Sun Q, Chen C, Anderson DJ, Perona P, Yue Y, Kennedy A (2021). The Multi-Agent Behavior Dataset: Mouse Dyadic Social Interactions. NeurIPS 2021 Datasets and Benchmarks track. arXiv:2104.02710v4. The target names doi:10.22002/D1.1991, which is the CaltechDATA record of the dataset (CalMS21); this paper is the one that record and the dataset describe. The full text (arXiv v4, with its appendix and datasheet) was used.

Dandiset. DANDI:001878, version draft. The dandiset has no published version, so the draft is the only one there is. It was last modified on 2026-06-25T18:32:10Z. To keep a changing draft from passing unnoticed, the helper module checks the blob id of each asset it reads against the one recorded when this notebook was written, and stops if it differs. The dandiset is a collection of conversions from three source datasets; for CalMS21 it holds one sequence, the Task 1 test sequence mouse071 (pose, annotations as bouts, and the video).

Data from elsewhere. The paper deposited the whole dataset on CaltechDATA (record s0vdx-0k302, version 1.0, the target DOI). The claims about the dataset as a whole (elsewhere) are tested on those files, streamed from the record's zips with range requests. The link claim and one pose-error claim (with inputs) use CaltechDATA's copy of mouse071 next to the dandiset's.

Code. The baseline code the paper links (gitlab.aicrowd.com/aicrowd/research/mab-e/mab-e-baselines) did not answer and no archived copy of the repository was found, and the top entries' code is not linked, so the model benchmarks are blocked.

The dandiset holds three NWB files with their videos, from three source datasets (keypoint-MoSeq, the Mlost benchmark and CalMS21); only sub-mouse071-resident-intruder is CalMS21. The other two have different pose series and frame counts (71,524 and 14,991 frames, against 23,810 here) and cite other DOIs (all printed above), so no CalMS21 recording is deposited twice. CalMS21 is linked as IsDerivedFrom, and the dandiset's licence is CC-BY-4.0, which matches the CaltechDATA record (shown below) but not the paper's datasheet, which gives CC-BY-NC-SA.

One session of one resident and intruder pair, 23,810 frames (13.2 min) at 30 Hz, all 14 series on the same rate and starting time. Positions are in pixels and lie within the stated 1024 x 570 image (x 5 to 991, y 9 to 563). Every confidence value is NaN: the MARS scores that CalMS21 distributes with the pose were not carried into the file, though the NWB field is present. The subject is a dyad stored as one Subject with sex U, strain C57BL/6 only (the BALB/c intruder is not recorded), and age P0D/; session_start_time is 2024-01-01T00:00, a placeholder, since CalMS21 gives no dates.

The catalogue lists attack, investigation, mount and other with codes 0 to 3, but its definition column is empty for all four, though the paper gives definitions (Appendix D.2). The bouts tile the session exactly: no gaps, edges on the 30 Hz frame grid, from 0 to 793.67 s, so each frame gets one label. This session has no attack. interanimal_distance is the distance between the two mice's centroids (mean of seven keypoints each), as described. centroid_speed is described as the speed of "the pose centroid (mean over keypoints)"; it is the speed of the mean of all 14 keypoints, which is the midpoint of the two mice, not the speed of either animal, and the bouts' mean_speed, peak_speed and immobility_fraction reduce it. Neither derived series is used below; speeds are computed per mouse.

started = time.time()
vinfo = calms21.video_info()
print("video:", vinfo)
STEP = 2  # decode at half resolution
energy = np.full(n, np.nan)
patch_rows = []
prev = None
n_decoded = 0
body = kp[:, :, :, [3, 4, 5]].mean(axis=3)  # neck and hips: (frames, mouse, x/y)
for i, img in calms21.video_frames(every=1, step=STEP):
    a = img.astype(np.int16)
    if prev is not None and i < n:
        energy[i] = np.abs(a - prev).mean()
    prev = a
    n_decoded += 1
    if i % 30 == 0 and i < n:
        row = {"frame": i, "sep": float(np.hypot(*(body[i, 0] - body[i, 1])))}
        for half in (4, 6, 12):  # patch half-widths in full-resolution pixels: 8, 12 and 24 px patches
            for m, name in enumerate(calms21.MICE):
                x, y = body[i, m] / STEP
                h = half // STEP  # half-width in decoded pixels; the patch is 2h decoded pixels wide
                x0, y0 = int(round(x - h)), int(round(y - h))  # centred on the body centre
                p = img[max(0, y0):y0 + 2 * h, max(0, x0):x0 + 2 * h]
                row[f"{name}_{2 * half}"] = float(p.mean()) if p.size else np.nan
        patch_rows.append(row)
patches = pd.DataFrame(patch_rows)
print(f"decoded {n_decoded} frames in {time.time() - started:.0f} s; pose frames {n}")

# Clock check: video motion energy against the speed of the two mice, over lags.
v_mice = np.nanmean([calms21.speed(cen[:, 0]), calms21.speed(cen[:, 1])], axis=0)
ok = np.isfinite(energy)
lags = np.arange(-15, 16)
xc = [stats.pearsonr(energy[ok][max(0, L):len(energy[ok]) + min(0, L)],
                     v_mice[ok][max(0, -L):len(v_mice[ok]) - max(0, L)])[0] for L in lags]
xc = pd.Series(xc, index=lags)
print("\ncorrelation of video motion energy with pose speed, by lag (video frame i against pose frame i - lag):")
print(xc.round(3).to_string())
print("peak at lag", int(xc.idxmax()), "frames, r =", round(xc.max(), 3), "; at lag 0 r =", round(xc[0], 3),
      "; at lag +-15 r =", round(xc[-15], 3), round(xc[15], 3))

The video is 1024 x 570 at 30 frames per second with 23,810 frames, as many as the pose. Its motion energy follows the speed of the mice most closely at lag 0 (printed above), so the video and the pose share one clock, to within a frame. The patches sampled here are used in resident-is-black.

In [6]:
# Clock check for the annotations: how well the nose-to-intruder distance separates investigation
# from other frames, with the labels shifted in time.
nose_d = calms21.nose_to_intruder(kp)


def auc(score, positive):
    r = stats.rankdata(score)
    n1, n0 = positive.sum(), (~positive).sum()
    return (r[positive].sum() - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)


shifts = np.r_[np.arange(-300, -30, 30), np.arange(-30, 31, 3), np.arange(60, 301, 30)]
rows = []
for k in shifts:
    lab = np.roll(labels, k)
    sel = np.isin(lab, ["investigation", "other"])
    if k > 0:
        sel[:k] = False
    elif k < 0:
        sel[k:] = False
    rows.append({"shift_frames": k, "auc_investigation_vs_other": auc(-nose_d[sel], lab[sel] == "investigation")})
shift_tab = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("shift_frames")
print(shift_tab.round(3).T.to_string())
best = shift_tab.auc_investigation_vs_other.idxmax()
print("best shift", best, "frames, AUC", round(shift_tab.auc_investigation_vs_other.max(), 3),
      "; at 0", round(shift_tab.loc[0].iloc[0], 3), "; at +-300 frames",
      round(shift_tab.loc[-300].iloc[0], 3), round(shift_tab.loc[300].iloc[0], 3))

The separation of investigation from other frames by the resident's nose distance is highest near zero shift and falls off with shifts of seconds, so the annotations share the pose's clock to within the printed resolution (3 frames near zero). This is consistent with the bouts being aligned to the pose; it does not resolve offsets of a frame or two.

leak = [h for h, sl in cross.items() if any(a.split("/")[0] == b.split("/")[0] and a != b for a in sl for b in sl)]

Every member's decompressed size and CRC matched the zip's directory (the helper checks both). In the labelled sets the length of the annotations equals the number of frames in the scores for every sequence, the frame counts of the keypoints and the scores agree in all 574 sequences, unlabeled ones included, and the vocabularies and annotator ids are those of Appendix C (Task 3 gives annotator ids 0, 2 and 6 by behavior, which the paper does not describe). Many sequences have identical keypoints over their whole length: the same recording deposited more than once, under other names and in other tasks (printed above): 574 sequences hold 450 distinct recordings. Most duplicates are Task 1 recordings that reappear in Task 3 (93 of the 109 Task 3 test sequences are Task 1 training recordings), and some cross the training and test splits of one task: four Task 2 recordings are in the training set of one of annotators 3 and 4 and the test set of the other, and five Task 1 test recordings, mouse071 among them, appear as six Task 3 training sequences (one recording is two of them). The paper says each sequence is an independent observation (Appendix B) and does not mention this. dataset-size counts each recording once under one of its readings; the counts and fractions of Tables 5 to 7 are per set, as the paper reports them.

format-keypoints¶

Each frame holds seven MARS keypoints (nose, left ear, right ear, neck, left hip, right hip, tail base) for each of two mice, the resident (mouse 0) and the intruder (mouse 1), in pixel coordinates of a 1024 x 570 image, at 30 Hz, with a confidence score from 0 to 1 for each keypoint.

In [8]:
expected_names = {f"{m}_{p}" for m in calms21.MICE for p in calms21.PARTS}
found = set(s["skeleton_nodes"])
print("14 series named for the seven parts of resident and intruder:", found == expected_names, f"({len(found)} nodes)")
print("units:", units, "; rates (Hz):", rates)
in_x = (kp[:, :, 0] >= 0) & (kp[:, :, 0] <= calms21.IMAGE_W)
in_y = (kp[:, :, 1] >= 0) & (kp[:, :, 1] <= calms21.IMAGE_H)
print(f"coordinates within the image: x {in_x.mean():.4f}, y {in_y.mean():.4f} of values")
print("pose dimensions stored (rows, cols):", s["pose_dimensions"], "; video", vinfo["width"], "x", vinfo["height"])
fin = np.isfinite(sc)
print(f"confidence values present: {fin.sum()} of {sc.size}" +
      (f"; range {sc[fin].min():.3f} to {sc[fin].max():.3f}" if fin.any() else ""))
positions_ok = found == expected_names and units == {"pixels"} and rates == {30.0} and in_x.all() and in_y.all()
scores_ok = fin.all() and (sc[fin] >= 0).all() and (sc[fin] <= 1).all()
print("positions meet the criterion:", positions_ok, "; confidence meets it:", scores_ok)

resident-is-black¶

Mouse 0, the resident, is the black C57Bl/6J mouse, and mouse 1, the intruder, is the white BALB/c mouse.

contact-during-social-behaviors¶

Close investigation, attack and mount are behaviors in which the resident is in close contact with the intruder; other frames include the animals apart.

pose-errors-close-fast¶

Errors in pose estimation are most common on frames when the two animals are in close contact or moving very quickly.

In [13]:
rng = np.random.default_rng(201)
SEGMENTS = {"nose-neck": (0, 3), "neck-tail": (3, 6), "ear-ear": (1, 2), "hip-hip": (4, 5)}
lengths = {(m, seg): np.hypot(*(kp[:, m, :, a] - kp[:, m, :, b]).T)
           for m in (0, 1) for seg, (a, b) in SEGMENTS.items()}


def error_flags(factor):
    flags = np.zeros(n, bool)
    for v in lengths.values():
        q1, q3 = np.percentile(v, [25, 75])
        flags |= (v < q1 - factor * (q3 - q1)) | (v > q3 + factor * (q3 - q1))
    return flags


# Speed of the faster mouse: running median of each mouse's speed, then the larger of the two.
v_fast = np.maximum(pd.Series(calms21.speed(cen[:, 0])).rolling(15, center=True, min_periods=1).median().values,
                    pd.Series(calms21.speed(cen[:, 1])).rolling(15, center=True, min_periods=1).median().values)
# Variant in the other order: the larger of the two speeds in each frame, then the running median.
v_fast_alt = pd.Series(np.fmax(calms21.speed(cen[:, 0]), calms21.speed(cen[:, 1]))).rolling(
    15, center=True, min_periods=1).median().values


def test(err, q, stat=np.mean, v=v_fast):
    out = {}
    close = d_cent <= np.quantile(d_cent, q)
    fast = v >= np.quantile(v, 1 - q)
    for nm, g in (("close", close), ("fast", fast)):
        d, lo, hi = calms21.block_bootstrap_diff(err.astype(float), g, 300, 2000, rng, stat=stat)
        out[nm] = (err[g].mean(), err[~g].mean(), d, lo, hi)
    return out


err = error_flags(3.0)
print(f"frames flagged as pose errors (factor 3): {err.sum()} of {n} ({err.mean():.4f})")
print("per segment and mouse:", {f"{calms21.MICE[m]} {seg}": int(((v < np.percentile(v, 25) - 3 * np.subtract(*np.percentile(v, [75, 25]))) |
      (v > np.percentile(v, 75) + 3 * np.subtract(*np.percentile(v, [75, 25])))).sum()) for (m, seg), v in lengths.items()})
print("close threshold (10%):", round(np.quantile(d_cent, 0.1), 1), "px; fast threshold (90%):",
      round(np.quantile(v_fast, 0.9), 1), "px/s")
rows = []
for factor in (3.0, 1.5):
    e = error_flags(factor)
    for q in (0.10, 0.05, 0.20):
        res = test(e, q)
        for nm, (a, b, d, lo, hi) in res.items():
            rows.append({"factor": factor, "fraction": q, "group": nm, "error_in_group": a, "error_elsewhere": b,
                         "diff": d, "ci_lo": lo, "ci_hi": hi})
errtab = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print("\nerror fraction in close / fast frames against the rest (main: factor 3, fraction 0.10):")
print(errtab.round(4).to_string(index=False))
rows = []
for q in (0.10, 0.05, 0.20):
    a, b, d, lo, hi = test(err, q, v=v_fast_alt)["fast"]
    rows.append({"fraction": q, "error_in_fast": a, "error_elsewhere": b, "diff": d, "ci_lo": lo, "ci_hi": hi})
print("\nvariant, fast frames by the running median of the larger speed (factor 3):")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(4).to_string(index=False))
by_label = pd.Series(err).groupby(labels).mean()
print("\nerror fraction by annotation label:", by_label.round(4).to_dict())
by_label_n = pd.Series(err).groupby(labels).sum()
print("flagged frames by annotation label:", {k: int(v) for k, v in by_label_n.items()},
      "; share of all flagged frames:", (by_label_n / err.sum()).round(3).to_dict())

Result: partially reproduced. Frames with an implausible body length are more common when the mice are closest: 0.131 of the closest 10% of frames against 0.016 of the rest (difference 0.115, 95% interval 0.064 to 0.179). They are less common, not more, in the fastest 10% of frames: 0.010 against 0.030 (difference -0.020, interval -0.033 to -0.008). Both directions hold at every threshold and factor shown. With the speed taken in the other order (larger speed per frame, then the running median) the fast frames still have fewer flags, with an interval that excludes 0 at 10% and 5% (-0.020, -0.033 to -0.008) and includes it at 20% (-0.011, -0.025 to 0.001). The error measure is a proxy chosen here, since the dandiset holds no confidence values. Mount holds the largest share of flagged frames (304 of 657, 0.463; error fraction 0.105 against 0.009 in other frames), where a hunched posture could give a real outlier; the flags are checked against the MARS confidence and the video under pose-errors-close-fast-confidence.

Result: reproduced. The sequence matches by name and has the same 23,810 frames; every keypoint coordinate is identical to CaltechDATA's (largest difference 0 px), and swapping the mice or the axes gives differences of about 895 px, so the order is the stated one. pose-errors-close-fast-confidence¶

Errors in pose estimation are most common on frames when the two animals are in close contact or moving very quickly, as shown by the MARS confidence scores.

In the closest 10% of frames, the 312 flagged frames have a lower MARS confidence than the 2,069 unflagged ones (median 0.574 against 0.657, difference -0.082, 95% interval -0.107 to -0.050), lowest for the intruder (0.521). 243 of the 312 are mount frames. In each of the eight flagged close frames drawn above, at least one segment drawn for a mouse runs across the other mouse or the background, which is a tracking error and not a posture (judged by eye on these eight frames only). So the flags in close frames mark mostly tracking errors, though the share of real postures among them is not measured.

Result: partially reproduced. The mean MARS confidence is lower in the closest 10% of frames (median 0.649 against 0.740, difference -0.091, 95% interval -0.107 to -0.074), most of all for the intruder (-0.149, resident -0.031). In the fastest 10% of frames it is higher, not lower (0.751 against 0.732, difference 0.018, interval 0.012 to 0.025). Both hold at the 5% and 20% thresholds, and with the speed taken in the other order (0.018, 95% interval 0.012 to 0.025, at 10%).

def count_table(df, paper):
    rows = []
    for g, (trf, trs, tef, tes) in paper.items():
        for split, pf, ps in (("train", trf, trs), ("test", tef, tes)):
            sub = df[(df.group == g) & (df.split == split)]
            rows.append({"group": g, "split": split, "frames": int(sub.n_annotations.sum()), "paper_frames": pf,
                         "sequences": len(sub), "paper_sequences": ps})
    t = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    t["frames_rel_diff"] = (t.frames - t.paper_frames) / t.paper_frames
    return t

table6-task1-label-fractions¶

In the Task 1 training set, 2.76% of frames are labelled attack, 28.9% investigation, 5.64% mount and 62.7% other.

In [20]:
PAPER_T6 = {"attack": (2.76, 0.005), "investigation": (28.9, 0.05), "mount": (5.64, 0.005), "other": (62.7, 0.05)}


def label_counts(df):
    tot = {}
    for counts in df.counts:
        for c, k in counts.items():
            tot[c] = tot.get(c, 0) + k
    return tot


def label_percent(df, vocab):
    tot = label_counts(df)
    allf = sum(tot.values())
    return {name: 100 * tot.get(code, 0) / allf for name, code in vocab.items()}, allf


rows = []
for reading, splits in (("a: train", ["train"]), ("b: train+test", ["train", "test"])):
    pct, allf = label_percent(t1[t1.split.isin(splits)], calms21.TASK1_VOCAB)
    cnt = label_counts(t1[t1.split.isin(splits)])
    for name, (val, tol) in PAPER_T6.items():

dataset-size¶

The unlabeled set has 282 videos and about 6 million frames; the dataset holds over 1 million annotated frames, over 70 hours of tracked poses and over 10 hours of frame-by-frame annotation.

Result: reproduced. The unlabeled set has 282 sequences and 5,952,058 frames, counted the same in the keypoints and the scores. Over all labelled sets there are 3,243,734 annotated frames (30.0 h), or 2,273,674 (21.1 h) with each recording counted once, and 85.2 h or 76.2 h of pose with the unlabeled set; so "over 1 million annotated frames", "over 10 hours of annotation" and "over 70 hours of pose" hold under readings (b) and (c). Task 1 alone has 769,845 annotated frames (7.1 h), and with the unlabeled set 62.2 h of pose, so none of the three holds under reading (a).

table10-task3-difficulty¶

On Task 3, classifier performance depends on the percentage of frames in which a behavior is observed and on its average bout duration, with shorter bouts giving lower performance.

In [24]:
BEHAVIORS = ["approach", "disengaged", "groom", "intromission", "mount_attempt", "sniff_face", "whiterearing"]
F1_BASELINE = [0.338, 0.195, 0.289, 0.721, 0.034, 0.358, 0.430]  # Table 10, baseline
F1_TASKPROG = [0.310, 0.198, 0.409, 0.609, 0.048, 0.274, 0.430]  # Table 10, baseline with task programming


def exact_spearman(x, y):
    # One-sided exact permutation p of Spearman's rho being at least the observed value.
    rx, ry = stats.rankdata(x), stats.rankdata(y)
    rho = stats.spearmanr(x, y)[0]
    perms = [stats.spearmanr(rx, np.array(p))[0] for p in itertools.permutations(ry)]
    return rho, float(np.mean(np.array(perms) >= rho - 1e-12))


rows, feats = [], {}
for split in ("train", "test"):
    pct, bout = [], []
    for b in BEHAVIORS:
        g = t3[(t3.group == b) & (t3.split == split)]
        p, _ = label_percent(g, {b: 1, "other": 0})
        runs = [r for d in g.runs for r in d.get(1, [])]
        pct.append(p[b]); bout.append(np.mean(runs) if runs else np.nan)
    feats[split] = pd.DataFrame({"percent_frames": pct, "mean_bout_frames": bout}, index=BEHAVIORS)
    for f1_name, f1 in (("baseline", F1_BASELINE), ("task programming", F1_TASKPROG)):
        for feat in ("percent_frames", "mean_bout_frames"):
            rho, p = exact_spearman(feats[split][feat].values, f1)
            rows.append({"split": split, "F1": f1_name, "feature": feat, "rho": rho, "p_one_sided": p})
for split, f in feats.items():
    print(f"{split} split:")
    print(f.assign(F1_baseline=F1_BASELINE).round(3).to_string())
corr = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print("\nSpearman correlations across the seven behaviors (exact one-sided permutation p):")
print(corr.round(3).to_string(index=False))

Result: partially reproduced. Across the seven behaviors, the baseline F1 rises with the percentage of labelled frames (Spearman 0.786, p = 0.024 on the training split; 0.929, p = 0.003 on the test split). It also rises with mean bout length, but not significantly (0.321, p = 0.249; 0.607, p = 0.083). With the task programming model's F1, the bout-length correlations are 0.536 (p = 0.118) and 0.679 (p = 0.055).

Summary¶

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How the analysis differs from the paper's. The paper describes a dataset and benchmarks models on it. The dandiset holds one of its sequences, so the claims about the dataset as a whole were tested on the CaltechDATA deposit. The paper gives no measure for "errors in pose estimation", "close contact" or "moving very quickly", nor a test of how Task 3 performance depends on frequency and bout length; the measures, thresholds and tests used here were fixed in the claims file before the analysis. Tolerances for counts and percentages of the deposited files are 0 and half a unit of the last reported digit, tighter than the protocol's default of 10%. No model was trained: the baseline code is not reachable and the paper leaves the architectures' settings to it.

What was found about the dandiset.

  • The CalMS21 part of the dandiset is one sequence of the dataset, Task 1 test sequence mouse071; its keypoints and frame annotations are identical to CaltechDATA's, and its video has the same frame count, size and rate as the pose and shares its clock.
  • The MARS confidence scores, which CalMS21 distributes with the pose, are missing: the field is present and every value is NaN.
  • The behavior catalogue has empty definitions, though the paper defines all three behaviors.
  • The subject is the dyad stored as one subject with strain C57BL/6 only, sex unknown and age P0D/; the session start time is a placeholder (2024-01-01). The dandiset's centroid_speed is the speed of the midpoint of the two mice, which its description does not make clear.
  • The video was re-encoded (184 MB against CaltechDATA's 964 MB for the same sequence); the dandiset does not say so.
  • The dandiset links the CalMS21 dataset DOI but not the paper (arXiv:2104.02710).

Outside the dandiset, the CaltechDATA deposit holds many recordings more than once across tasks, including across the training and test splits, which the paper does not mention; one Table 5 count differs from the data by 10 frames; and the paper's datasheet gives a different licence (CC-BY-NC-SA) from the deposit and the dandiset (CC-BY 4.0), and says the raw videos are not included while Section 3.1 and the deposit include the Task 1 videos.
